1:
Where this begins and what it is are settled differently before a word is expounded. Gill marks the turn from the captivity predicted in the preceding chapter into the more evangelical part of the prophecy, reaching from the coming of the Baptist to the second coming, beginning with comforts and ending with them. Clarke reads the opening as the restoration of the church, with a harbinger sent ahead to clear the road as before eastern kings, and holds that the later scriptures authorise referring the words to the gospel. Calvin reconstructs the occasion: the prophet, making no impression on his generation, turns to posterity, and probably wrote when the captivity was near, so as not to leave the church at his death without hope. Ellicott opens with a declared assumption rather than an argument, that the poem which follows is Isaiah's own, and refers the question of authorship elsewhere. Keil and Delitzsch answer with architecture: the second half of the book falls into three parts of three times three addresses each, an arrangement scarcely disputed since it was pointed out in the eighteen-thirties.

Who is told to comfort is less disputed than pressed. Wesley says shortly: ye prophets and ministers. Henry widens it in three steps — it warranted this prophet to encourage the good of his own day, directed the prophets who would live through the captivity, and puts gospel ministers in mind of their business. Ellicott keeps it to the exile, addressing prophets whom Isaiah foresees working towards its close, and traces their influence in later prophets. Calvin turns the address round: God does not so much exhort the prophets to courage as convey to believers an assured hope, that they may bear the delay until the prophets come with the message.

On speaking to the heart they converge and colour it differently. Gill wants a cordial, proclaimed aloud so she may hear. Keil and Delitzsch trace the idiom through words that win a heart and a brother inspiring confidence in brothers. Calvin gives the psychology: the heart recoils from sad news and runs to meet what is agreeable, so to speak to the heart is to speak according to its wish.

Who Jerusalem is divides the reading. Gill takes her for the Gospel church, and reports the Jewish reading that makes her the congregation of Israel. Keil and Delitzsch keep the holy city itself, thought of with the people belonging to it. Ellicott hears in my people an echo of the earlier prophet, where those once named not-my-people are brought back; and notes that saith your God is a formula peculiar to Isaiah and common to both halves of the book.

The double is the crux, and every voice bends it somewhere. Keil and Delitzsch render the clauses as affliction ended, debt paid, double received from the LORD's hand. Ellicott works the first two: the warfare is a campaign, the time of war standing for sufferings that are not war, so the exile was one long war with enemies worse than the conquerors — a word applied elsewhere to the battle of life, which he counts among the parallels between this book and that of Job; and the pardon is strictly a debt paid off. Clarke refuses the plain sense outright. It cannot be reconciled with divine justice, which always punishes less than iniquity deserves, that God punished these sins in double proportion; a consolatory message asks rather for a promise of ample recompense, and he adds a word or two to his version to get it — blessings double to the punishment. He reports besides the Jewish reading that the double is the two captivities, the Babylonian and the one still endured. Wesley takes the middle: not twice what her sins deserved, but enough to answer the design of the chastisement, which was to humble and reform them and warn others by their example.
3:
Where the wilderness belongs changes the sentence. Ellicott says Hebrew parallelism requires a different punctuation, the words going with the command and not the crier: a voice of one crying, In the wilderness prepare ye. Keil and Delitzsch render it the same way, and Clarke repunctuates to the same effect. Gill keeps the English attachment and locates the crying in the wilderness. Calvin takes the word metaphorically for the desolation then existing, without denying an allusion to the road between Judea and Babylon.

Who the crier is turns on how far forward one reads. Gill rejects the Jewish reading that makes it the Holy Ghost and takes it for the Baptist; and he says what kind of voice — not a voice and nothing else, like the nightingale, but a teaching voice, the voice of a prophet. Ellicott takes the opposite pleasure in the word: the herald is not named, and the Baptist, taking the verse as the definition of his mission, was content to efface himself and be a voice or nothing. Henry allows the prophets among the captives first and then insists on the Baptist; Wesley says it relates immediately to the return from Babylon and principally to the Messiah; Calvin puts the objection he expects — you promise consolation, but where are the prophets?

The road-making they take from one custom and document differently. Clarke describes eastern monarchs sending harbingers ahead and pioneers to open the passes, notes that the Latins called such officers stratores, and quotes a scholar calling the Baptist the strator of the Messiah. Wesley gives the same custom and reads the sense off it: God will so dispose men's hearts and order the world's affairs as to make way. Ellicott reaches for something harder — the titanic engineering of the East's kingly road-makers, who boast in the Assyrian inscriptions of roads cut through trackless deserts — and puts the wilderness between the Euphrates and Judah.

Whether the levelling is commanded or foretold divides the grammarians from the rest. Keil and Delitzsch take the summons as continuing in a commanding tone: let every valley be exalted, let the rugged be made a plain. Calvin says the words might properly be imperative, and reports others taking the command as running on from the chapter's opening. Gill and Ellicott keep the future. Clarke stops at a word: crooked is the usual rendering, but he thinks the sense unsupported and the parallelism better if the hilly country is made level and the precipices a plain.

What is levelled is the next difference. Gill takes it parabolically: those bowed with guilt raised up, the self-righteous brought low. Ellicott says the parable is hardly veiled and gives four in a line: the meek exalted, the proud brought low, wrong ways set right, rough natures smoothed — the true work of every follower of the Baptist. Calvin keeps it on the deliverance: no difficulty can stop the Lord restoring his Church.

The glory closes the passage, and Ellicott leaves it a question: did the prophet think of a glory-cloud like the one he saw in the temple, or had he risen to a glory of character and will? On the seeing he is definite — the revelation is for mankind and not Israel only, and the phrase all flesh, meeting us here first, marks the growing catholicity of his thought. Gill takes the glory for Christ himself; Keil and Delitzsch make the unveiling follow the prepared way; Calvin says the Church's deliverance down to Christ might be called a second creation of the world. Clarke argues a textual case: the Greek adds the salvation of our God, the sentence being abrupt without it since the verb wants its object, and though the omission is older than the ancient versions the words stand in every Greek copy and are acknowledged in the gospel, so he thinks them genuine.
6:
A second voice speaks and someone answers it, and who they are is disputed. Gill sets aside two Jewish readings that make it an angel or the voice of prophecy, and takes it for the Lord's own voice to the prophet, or rather to any gospel minister, since without such an order none can preach lawfully. Calvin marks the same change: the earlier voice was the prophets', this is God commanding them, and the distinction matters so we may know when the Lord commands and when his ministers execute — with the consequence that what the prophets utter is to be received as reverently as if God thundered from heaven. Keil and Delitzsch count further and hear a second voice and then a third in conversation, the second celebrating the promise and appointing a preacher of its endurance. Ellicott makes the questioner the prophet himself; Wesley agrees, God speaking to his ministers and the prophet answering.

What blows on the grass is the sharpest disagreement here. Clarke calls a wind of Jehovah a plain Hebraism for a strong wind, and observes that a hot wind in the east destroys every green thing; he adds that two manuscripts omit the divine name altogether. Ellicott agrees and argues it from the parable — we are still inside the figure and the agency is destructive rather than quickening, so a wind of Jehovah is a storm-blast tearing the grass up. Calvin allows that reading, since wind is called the Spirit of God elsewhere and a gust spoils a field's beauty, but inclines to take the metaphor as fitted to the subject: men with all their gifts are grass because the Spirit of God will carry them off with one breath.

Clarke also reports that the verse may not belong here at all. The whole of it is wanting in three of one collator's manuscripts and five of another's, in a very correct and ancient copy of his own, and in the Greek and the Arabic; and on the following clause he notes that one version seems to have read a slightly different Hebrew.

Ellicott sets the image in two frames. One is literary: the fading flower recalls the well-known line that the generations of men are as the generations of leaves, and the thought is another of the parallels he keeps finding with the book of Job. The other is biographical, offered to account for the naturalness of the sentiment — a man in extreme old age looking back over the generations he had outlived and forward to the fall of one great monarchy after another would think in these terms.

Why the withering is said twice they answer differently. Gill takes the repetition as raising attention to a matter of importance and confirming it. Calvin gives it a double office: it brings the glory of the flesh to nothing and at the same moment carries a consolation, since God casts his people down only to raise them immediately, and the one comfort left is that we are frail while the word of the Lord is durable and eternal, held out like a hand.

What that word is they take at different widths. Ellicott makes it primarily the prophetic word revealing God's will, but says it takes in every manifestation of his being. Wesley draws the practical conclusion the passage is built for: God's word is like himself, immutable and irresistible, and since it is the mouth of the LORD and not of man that has spoken these things, there is no doubting they will be fulfilled. Keil and Delitzsch put the contrast as the point of the whole exchange — grass withers and flower fades, yet the word of our God will stand for ever.
9:
Whether Zion carries the news or receives it is the first quarrel, and the feminine participle is used on both sides. Gill prefers the reading that makes her the recipient, as agreeing better with the rest of the verse. Clarke argues it at length: the true construction makes Zion the receiver, not the publisher, though the publisher reading has prevailed, and he supplies the word daughter to carry the feminine into English, since the image depends on it. Ellicott takes the same participle to prove the opposite: since it is feminine, and no female herald but Jerusalem has appeared, Zion herself must bear the news to the cities of Judah. Wesley says it flatly, Zion the publisher and the cities the hearers; Calvin has the message given first to Zion and now spread through the other cities; Henry keeps both, notice given to the remnant in Zion and to the captives who belonged to her.

Clarke grounds his reading in a custom: the office of announcing and celebrating such glad tidings — a great public success, a signal victory — belonged peculiarly to the women, and that practice fixes the image and requires the feminine.

Ellicott stops instead over a word: it is not without emotion, he says, that one notes here the first occurrence of the term which, passing through the Greek into the later scriptures, has had so fruitful a history as the word carrying the message of good tidings to mankind.

How the LORD comes is a translation dispute. Keil and Delitzsch refuse the rendering with strength, which the Greek and Targum give, and take the particle as one of essence: he comes in the energy of a strong one, his arm ruling for him. Ellicott reads it the same way and notes that the arm is a favourite Isaianic word for power, the doubled divine name characteristic of both halves. Calvin reports a third construction that has stood in respectable company, against the strong one — against the nations, to punish them.

What he brings with him divides them along a line they do not draw. Clarke makes the reward what God bestows and will pay to his faithful servants, held ready and out in front to encourage those who wait. Ellicott supports the same from the noun, which carries the sense of a recompense for the faithful worker. Wesley will not have it one-sided: he comes furnished with recompenses of blessing for his friends and vengeance for his enemies, and explains the idiom, that what is before a man is in scripture what lies in his power. Gill hears the second coming in it, when the reward is given to every man according to his works.

The shepherd closes the passage, and Keil and Delitzsch mark what the change of image does: the prophet turns from the judicial side to the redeeming, showing the love by an example — the lambs not long born, and the ewes giving suck rather than the sucklings. Clarke reads the last clause as the nursing ewes gently led, and grounds it twice: in the plea a patriarch made to his brother that overdriving the flocks giving suck would kill them, and in a traveller's account of eastern herdsmen forced to move often because their flocks eat down a camp so fast. Ellicott reaches independently for the same patriarch's plea, and sets the psalm and the gospel chapter beside the verse as the great embodiments of the thought. Calvin explains why an image was needed: God works in innumerable ways and the hearer might have been left in suspense as to which work was meant, and the shepherd expresses an infinite love in one who does not refuse to stoop so low. Gill fills in whose flock it is — one flock, little, and often a flock of slaughter, held by the Father's gift and the shepherd's purchase.
12:
Why the greatness is described here they agree on. Henry gives three reasons: to encourage captives to depend on him though weak and their oppressors strong, to hold them from other gods since none compare, and to fill those who receive the glad tidings with awe. Wesley says it shorter: the discourse of infinite power assures them God was able to do what he promised. Calvin makes the point defensively: an ignorant reader would think the prophet crowds together unfinished sentences, but the object explains the manner, for this is a support of faith, and Israel is meant to know this shield alone sufficient.

Whose greatness it is divides one voice from the rest. Gill takes the whole account of power and wisdom to be Christ's, given to show him equal to the redemption he has undertaken, and that in condescending to a shepherd's office he lost no dignity as a divine person; and he carries it through, so that it is the Spirit of Christ whom none counselled in creation. Keil and Delitzsch, Ellicott and Calvin keep the questions on Jehovah, the first recalling his omnipotence and the second his omniscience.

What the Spirit is in the second question is disputed. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch both reach back to creation, the Spirit that moved on the waters, with none beside him to advise. Ellicott holds the word, used in a lower sense a few verses earlier, is here clothed with a divine personality, answering to the figure of wisdom in the proverbs. He then sets it against the neighbours: an eastern cosmogony might have its chief god calling lesser deities into counsel, where this prophet finds no counsellor but one essentially one with the Eternal. Calvin turns it on the reader: carnal sense limits God's power to human means, so whenever we cannot see how God will do a thing we doubt it.

Ellicott keeps finding one neighbourhood for the language. The measuring and weighing supply another parallel with the book of Job; the Creator is the great work-master of the universe, ordering all things by number and weight and measure; and the second question's words belong to the vocabulary of the wisdom books.

What Lebanon's insufficiency proves is the one real split. Wesley and Calvin take it of worship: the whole forest could not afford wood or beasts enough for a sacrifice answerable to what God deserves, and Calvin thinks the prophet turns to worship deliberately, to deepen reverence. Keil and Delitzsch put it the same way and mark the word, which means what suffices rather than what is required. Ellicott adds why Lebanon in particular: it is the type of the forests that supplied wood for burnt offerings, in which Judah was poor. Clarke alone turns the verse toward atonement: he asks whether the prophet does not mean that all the offerings that could be made were insufficient to atone for sin, so the nations are nothing not merely for his immensity but for their inability to atone, and therefore the Redeemer was to come.

In what sense the nations are nothing is pressed hardest by Calvin, who raises the objection himself: it seems absurd to call them nothing, since God created them that they might be something; but it is said by comparison, and because the depravity of the human mind obscures the divine majesty and sets above it what ought to be subject, so in that contest we may boldly say whatever is compared with God is worthless. Gill puts it as nonentity beside the Being of beings. Wesley keeps to the figures: dust cleaving to the balance without altering the weight, and isles that are the vast countries reached from Judea by sea. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both hear in the last word the chaos of the creation account, Ellicott counting it among the prophet's favourite terms.
18:
Who the challenge is aimed at they settle alike. Keil and Delitzsch address it not to idolaters but to Israelites needing arming against a seduction most of mankind had yielded to; Gill calls it an antidote against idolatry in Babylon; Calvin has the prophet turn from the Gentiles to his own people. Ellicott notes the appeal goes to the primary intuitions of mankind rather than to the commandments of the law. Henry sorts the folly in two: representing God by creatures, and putting creatures in his place.

Ellicott sets the prophet beside the apostle who used the same argument at Athens: sarcastic and declamatory here, pitying there, with an indulgent allowance for times of ignorance, the difference lying partly in the two men and partly in their hearers, who had known nothing better than their fathers' worship.

The idol shop is drawn in detail: Gill has the founder melting metal into a mould, Keil and Delitzsch the plating and melted silver chains, Ellicott the chains fastening the image to the wall. Ellicott then draws a conclusion about the writer: the reigns the prophet had lived through must have supplied this picture as fully as living in Babylon would have.

Then the poor man's god. Gill reports two constructions besides the usual: the man set over the oblation, and a tree that will not rot. Clarke draws the moral: the rich made theirs of gold, the poor of wood. Ellicott says the abrupt transition shows idolatry at two extremes — the elaborate art kings delighted in, and a rude fetish, a useless log on its wide base. On what that stability means he and Wesley part, for Wesley reads the same immovability as impotence, an image that cannot stir to help you. Calvin looks past both to the cause: men wish to enjoy the presence of God, and that wish is the source of idolatry, since God is present not by an idol but by his word and Spirit.

The circle of the earth divides the cosmology. Gill takes it of the globe itself, hung as a ball in the air rather than a flat plain, then the Jewish view making heaven the circle and earth its centre. Wesley keeps the earth round and adds that scripture speaks likewise of the circle of heaven and of the deep. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch place the circle overhead, the vault arching over the earth. On the curtain Clarke quotes a traveller's awning spread on ropes across a court in summer; Ellicott finds a clearer perception of space than the older term for the firmament gave: the heavens a filmy gauze, the curtains of God's tent.

The princes go the way of the grass. Gill asks where the old monarchies are now. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott render the clause alike — the rulers are hardly planted, hardly sown, before the storm carries them off like stubble — and Ellicott draws the point: such are empires beside God's eternity, so soon withered we cannot say they were planted. Clarke notes several versions read the particle without its conjunction.

The challenge returns, and then the stars. Calvin says the repetition is made in indignation, lest the Jews detract from God's power because they had been so long captive. Ellicott, noting the verb for created as a mark of these chapters, reads the marshalling of the host as an expansion of the divine name of hosts — a general who knows every soldier by name. Clarke passes on a rabbinic saying, that a man capable of meditating on the revolutions of the heavenly bodies and not doing it is unworthy to be named among men. Calvin admits the prophet seems to linger on what nobody disputes, and answers that we are such ungrateful judges of divine power that one man's empty mask oftener terrifies us than all of this strengthens.
27:
Who is complaining they settle much alike. Gill takes the captives of the older commentators, or else the church under Rome pagan or papal, repining inwardly and aloud. Keil and Delitzsch narrow it: not the idolaters just rebuked, but the despondent who still desire salvation, cast down and not in utter despair. Their way is their thorny way of life, their right their good right against oppressors, and God appeared to notice neither. Wesley puts the grievance plainly: he takes no notice of my prayers and tears. Calvin allows such murmurs were probably heard, and that the prophet may be providing for posterity.

Henry hears the doubling and makes it the fault: bad to have evil thoughts rise in the mind, worse to sanction them and turn them into words. He divides the despair in two: God would not heed them, their way hidden as a man is hedged in, and God could not help them, their case past relief. The names are the answer; Henry says they should shame them, recalling an ancestor who found God faithful in all his straits, Calvin hearing in them the covenant. Ellicott adds the ground: this eternity is no transient favour, no capricious will.

The reproof for ignorance is pressed by all. Gill lists where they might have learned better: the history of the church in every age, the experience of good men, the Scriptures. Calvin makes them doubly guilty, taught by numerous benefits and by the word, excessively unteachable if they have profited nothing. Keil and Delitzsch give the reason to know: the Creator of the ends of the earth had Babylon well within his vision and power. Ellicott notes the questions repeat the earlier ones, now put to the Israel of God rather than to mankind.

Calvin argues from the word eternal: what is eternal never changes or decays, and were this seated deeply in us there would be no room for distrust. Ellicott raises a question about the writer: had the prophet come to feel his own earlier phrase about men wearying God too boldly anthropomorphic? He traces the unsearchable understanding to the book of Job, and to the apostle's mind at the great doxology. Clarke keeps to the text, where two dozen manuscripts and the ancient versions read the conjunction.

Strength is given where it is confessed absent. Ellicott says the faint receive it pre-eminently, their consciousness of weakness being the condition of receiving it; Calvin makes it strict, since hearts not deeply moved by a conviction of weakness cannot receive seasonable assistance; Keil and Delitzsch reduce the requirement to faith alone. Who the failing youths are then divides them. Gill takes them of men in the prime of strength who glory in it, reports the Targum and the Jewish commentators reading them of the wicked, and applies it to the emperors who persecuted the church and the antichristian states; Henry turns it inward, to those who trust their own sufficiency and so neither exert themselves to the utmost nor seek grace. Wesley says only, the youngest and strongest, left to themselves; Ellicott marks the second word as the age of highest vigour.

The eagle draws out the most. Clarke reports the old opinion that the bird moults in age and renews its feathers with its youth, cites a Latin father and a rabbi's tale of the eagle flying near the sun every tenth year, then declines to adjudicate: enough for a poet, profane or sacred, to have popular opinion behind an image used for ornament. Ellicott holds the same belief about the plumage but prefers lifting up their wings. Calvin reports the Hebrew idiom of exchanging strength and makes waiting mean patience: violent men dash themselves to pieces by their eagerness, while godly vigour is quietly renewed. Gill spends his on the waiting itself, as beggars who knock, meet repulses, and keep their place.
